title: Forgiving the gunman (1983)
hook: John Paul II visits in prison the man who shot him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solidarity: a shipyard gate, a round table, and a country changed. Your line was without violence. Which worker did you thank? Today, the pope meets violence face to face. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

Cameras catch the scene, but not the words. Two chairs pulled close in a small prison cell in Rome. One man in white, one in a prisoner's clothes. They lean in until their heads nearly touch, and they talk quietly for a long time. At one point the man in white holds the other man's hand. The prisoner is Mehmet Ali Ağca. Some time before, in Saint Peter's Square, in front of a crowd, he raised a pistol and shot the man now sitting beside him. The visitor is John Paul the Second.
screen: `A CELL IN ROME, TWO CHAIRS.` → `THEY TALK FOR A LONG TIME.` → `THE GUNMAN AND THE POPE.`

segments.voice: Four moments make this story. First, the square. John Paul was riding slowly through the crowd in an open car when shots rang out. He was badly wounded and rushed to a hospital, and for a time it was not clear he would live. The gunman was caught on the spot. Second, the hospital. Within days, still weak, the pope spoke to the world by radio from his bed. He asked people to pray for the brother who had shot him, and said that he had sincerely forgiven him. Not the gunman. The brother. Third, the cell. Later, after his recovery, he went to the prison himself. He did not send a letter or a bishop. He went to the cell, sat down, and talked with the man. Afterward he said that what they talked about would remain a secret between them, and that he had spoken to him as a brother whom he had pardoned and who had his complete trust. Jesus, in Matthew's Gospel, names prison visits among the things done for him. In the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." Fourth, what forgiveness did not do. Ağca stayed in prison for years after the visit. The pope did not pretend the shooting was small or that justice didn't matter. Catholic teaching holds forgiveness and justice side by side: you can release a debt in your heart and still let the courts do their work. Two chairs, two men, a held hand. What was said in that cell, they kept between them.
screen: `SHOTS IN SAINT PETER'S SQUARE.` · `FROM A HOSPITAL BED: MY BROTHER.` · `HE WENT TO THE CELL.` · `FORGIVENESS AND JUSTICE, BOTH.` · then, large: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse forgiving someone face to face. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who hurt you, not the deepest wound, something you can hold today. Picture two chairs, close. Picture them in the other one. You don't have to say it's fine. You can name what happened, and then, if you're ready, say: I forgive you. If you're not ready, notice that, and leave the chair there for another day. Forgiving never means putting yourself in harm's way. If you pray, you can pray for them, as the pope did, by name. The bell holds the time.
Forgiving the gunman. John Paul the Second, shot in Saint Peter's Square, forgave Mehmet Ali Ağca and went to visit him in prison.

Your line: he went to the cell. Today, if it's safe and you're ready, take one step toward the person in the other chair: a message, a call, or just their name in a prayer. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics who volunteer in prison ministry visit inmates, often bringing Communion and listening, and some point to John Paul II's visit to Ağca and to Jesus's words in Matthew 25 as their pattern.

notes: Claims rule: no dates spoken; the title's year stays in the title only. No length of the meeting given ('a long time').
Confirm: open vehicle in Saint Peter's Square; 'not clear he would live'; Ağca caught at the scene.
Confirm the hospital message: prayer for 'the brother who shot me, whom I have sincerely forgiven' (paraphrased).
Confirm remarks after the Rebibbia visit: what we said is a secret between us; spoke as to a brother whom I have pardoned and who has my complete trust (paraphrased).
'Held the other man's hand': confirm from photographs.
